title: Conversation state snapshotting - arch jam notes
content:
Attendees: Marcus Li (lead), Aisha Patel, Diego Martinez, Rina Kaur, Oliver Chen, Priya Nair

Goal: Capture the outcomes of the architecture jam where we reviewed options for snapshotting conversation state across the serving runtime (hosted, dedicated, private). We focused on latency-sensitive checkpoints, durability for LLM session resumption, migration paths between model variants, and operational complexity.

Context / why this matters:
- Customers rely on conversational continuity (long-running chats, tool calls, multi-turn prompts).
- Current approach: per-worker in-memory KV + prefix caching. When workers restart or are evicted, we either lose context or fall back to recomputing from history which is expensive.
- Need: low-latency resume, bounded recovery time for SLOs, minimal extra cost for hosted customers, and clear privacy controls for Private deployments.

Agenda:
1) Quick recap of problem and constraints (5m)
2) Three design proposals walkthrough (30m)
3) Tradeoff matrix and perf/cost concerns (15m)
4) Decision & migration strategy outline (10m)
5) Actions and owners (10m)

Proposals reviewed:
- Option A — Ephemeral local snapshots with opportunistic upload
  - Each worker keeps frequent local checkpoints (delta of KV & short history) to local SSD. On a graceful shutdown or low-latency idle, worker pushes a trimmed snapshot to S3-backed blobstore with TTL. On crash, fallback to replay from upstream prefix cache + last persisted snapshot.
  - Pros: minimal steady-state cost; lowest read latency for cold start when snapshot is local; simple for Dedicated/Private where node storage is available.
  - Cons: longer recovery for crashes (need to wait for upload), complexity around crash-consistency, not ideal for strict privacy (uploaded snapshot).

- Option B — Centralized session-store (strongly consistent)
  - External store (managed Redis/consensus) holds canonical conversation snapshot per session. Workers read/write with optimistic concurrency. Durable across restarts and supports immediate failover.
  - Pros: fastest recovery, simple semantics, good for multi-worker routing and stateful handoffs.
  - Cons: adds steady-state latency on hot path unless heavily cached; operational cost and single additional service to manage; private deployments may resist external managed services (but can be co-located).

- Option C — Hybrid delta-checkpointing + append-only WAL with compaction (recommended direction)
  - Fast local in-memory deltas applied to worker state + append-only per-session WAL pushed to a tiered storage: local SSD for recent deltas (hot), then object store for durable shards. Periodic compaction produces versioned full snapshots. Metadata (seqno, model-version, shard-id) lives in small, cheap metadata store (Dynamo/Sheets-like) for lookups.
  - Pros: low on-path latency (local deltas), fast warm-start from local SSD, durable recovery from object store, supports cross-worker handoff by replaying WAL to new worker, and compaction keeps storage costs manageable.
  - Cons: complexity in compaction, metadata coordination, and migration logic between model variants.

Tradeoff matrix (summary):
- Latency impact: A (low), B (medium on hot path), C (low if local SSD present)
- Durability: A (medium), B (high), C (high after compaction)
- Operational complexity: A (low), B (medium-high), C (high)
- Cost: A (low), B (high), C (medium)
- Privacy control (Private deploys): A (good control), B (depends on store), C (good if object store is customer-managed)

Discussion highlights and points raised:
- Rina: For Hosted, the steady-state cost of a centralized store (Option B) could be significant; prefer hybrid where we can tune TTLs and compaction windows per-customer tier.
- Diego: Concern about ordering and seqno gaps when model-variant rollouts happen mid-conversation — need a clear migration API (model-version pinning + replay semantics).
- Priya: Private deployments must have an option to keep snapshots on customer-managed object stores or encrypted-only buckets (no external uploads).
- Oliver: Suggested we prototype compaction jobs as a serverless pipeline (lambda-like) to avoid long-running compaction nodes in Dedicated.

Decision (consensus): Move forward with Option C (Hybrid delta-checkpoint + WAL + tiered storage), with these constraints:
- Default behavior for Hosted: short local SSD window (30s-5m configurable) + rapid push of WAL to object store; compaction window = 6h by default for standard tier, configurable per-customer.
- Dedicated: enable longer local SSD retention and faster compaction since capacity predictable.
- Private: support customer-managed object stores and an encrypted-only snapshot mode (snapshots never leave customer VPC unless explicitly enabled).
- Provide a compatibility shim so older workers without snapshotting still function (fall back to prefix replay).

Open design questions to resolve in follow-ups:
- Snapshot metadata schema: minimal required fields (session_id, last_seqno, model_version, snapshot_ts, compaction_root_hash, storage_locator) — concrete schema needed.
- Compaction heuristics: size threshold vs time-based; how to atomic-swap snapshot roots without inconsistent reads.
- Read-after-write consistency SLA: what timeframe until a newly written delta is considered discoverable by handoff worker?
- Cost model: rough t-shirt sizing for storage and egress for Hosted tier.

Implementation plan (phased):
1) Spike (2 weeks) — prototype delta WAL writer + local SSD hot window; measure write/append latency and local recovery time. Owner: Aisha (deliver prototype + perf notes by 2025-03-28).
2) Metadata schema & API (1 week) — draft snapshot metadata proto, migration API for model-version pinning, and handoff flow. Owner: Diego (API draft by 2025-03-21).
3) Durable push & object store integration (2 weeks) — S3-compatible writer supporting customer-managed endpoints; encryption-at-rest integration. Owner: Rina (PR + integration tests by 2025-04-11).
4) Compaction PoC (3 weeks) — serverless compactor that consumes WALs and emits versioned full snapshots, with atomic swap of metadata root. Owner: Oliver (PoC + runbook by 2025-04-18).
5) End-to-end QA + stress tests (2 weeks) — warm/cold-start SLO tests, eviction & crash-recovery tests, multi-worker handoff. Owner: Priya (tests + results by 2025-05-02).

Action items (short list):
- Aisha: Build WAL + local SSD hot-window prototype (due 2025-03-28).
- Diego: Draft snapshot metadata proto & handoff API (due 2025-03-21).
- Rina: Implement object-store writer with encrypted uploads & test endpoints (due 2025-04-11).
- Oliver: Prototype serverless compactor and document compaction semantics (due 2025-04-18).
- Priya: Create QA plan and SLO test harness (due 2025-05-02).
- Marcus: Create RFC doc summarizing decision, add cost/ROI appendix, and route for review by infra-security (due 2025-03-20).

Notes / heuristics we agreed to follow:
- Keep on-path writes cheap: critical path should not block on remote durable writes. WAL append should be local-SSD-first and async-push to object store.
- Provide explicit opt-in for synchronous durability when customers request (e.g., high-assurance enterprise plan).
- Expose snapshot TTL & compaction knobs via per-customer config in UI and API.
- Preserve backwards compatibility: workers should exchange fallback markers so older workers can be routed appropriately.

Risks called out:
- Compaction bugs could produce incompatible snapshot roots; will require strong end-to-end tests and a canary migration strategy.
- Private deployments have variable infrastructure (no SSDs, restricted outbound). We need a minimal fallback (append-only to customer-managed object store) that works without local SSD.

Follow-ups and owners recap (with Slack links):

- Spike branch (Aisha): https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tree/wip/wal-snapshots
- Jira tickets: JIRA-1234 (design), JIRA-1256 (compaction PoC), JIRA-1267 (qa harness)

End of notes.
